Monmouth. On June 28, 1778, the Continental Army and British forces clashed at Monmouth Courthouse in New Jersey. This was a rare mid-summer engagement, as armies usually campaigned only in warmer months but settled in winter quarters. American General Charles Lee launched the initial attack, but it was poorly coordinated and broke down. He retreated despite having superior numbers. Washington arrived and rallied the troops with a stirring appearance on the battlefield, personally intervening at a critical moment. His presence inspired the American forces, who formed a solid defensive line. American artillery, particularly under Henry Knox, played a crucial role in stabilizing the line and forcing British withdrawal. The British, unable to break the American position, chose to withdraw toward New York rather than continue the engagement. The fighting remained indecisive—neither side achieved a decisive victory—but the British withdrew and the Americans claimed a moral and strategic victory by denying Howe an easy campaign. Charles Lee was later court-martialed for his mishandling of the battle and his retreat in the face of the enemy.
